'''James Kakalios''' (born December 27, 1958)<ref name="Kakalios CV">{{cite web|url=http://www.physics.umn.edu/people/kakalios.html|title=James Kakalios|publisher=University of Minnesota School of Physics and Astronomy|accessdate=July 24, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120405065509/http://www.physics.umn.edu/people/kakalios.html|archive-date=April 5, 2012}}</ref> is a physics professor and head of the School of Physics and Astronomy at the [[University of Minnesota]]. Known within the scientific community for his work with [[Amorphous solid|amorphous]] [[semiconductors]], [[granular material]]s, and [[1/f noise]], he is known to the general public as the author of the book ''[[The Physics of Superheroes]]'', which considers [[comic book]] [[superhero]]es from the standpoint of fundamental physics.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.physicsofsuperheroes.com/|title=James Kakalios - U. of Minnesota Physics Professor and Author of The Physics of Superheroes|website=www.physicsofsuperheroes.com|access-date=2017-09-09}}</ref>

==Biography==
Kakalios earned his B.S. degree from [[City College of New York]] in 1979 and his M.S. and [[PhD]] degrees from the [[University of Chicago]] in 1982 and 1985.<ref name="Kakalios CV"/> He began his comic book collection as a [[graduate student]] as a way to relieve stress. At Minnesota, he taught a freshman seminar that focused on the physics of superheroes as a way to motivate students to think about physics. This course gained great popularity as an enticing alternative to the typical inclined planes and pulleys of physics.{{citation needed|date=October 2014}}[[File:James Kakalios with Lord Adebowale.jpg|thumb|James Kakalios (left) with the [[University of Lincoln]] (UK) Chancellor [[Victor Adebowale, Baron Adebowale|Lord Victor Adebowale]] (right) after receiving Honorary DSc degree. 7th September 2017, Lincoln, UK.]]The seminar was a great success, leading to articles in popular magazines including ''[[People magazine|People]]'', lectures on the subject, and publication of ''The Physics of Superheroes''.  In his talks, favorite examples are the [[The Night Gwen Stacy Died|death]] of [[Gwen Stacy]] ([[Spider-Man]]'s girlfriend), "can [[Superman]] jump over tall buildings and what does this tell us about Krypton?", the high-velocity actions of [[Flash (comics)|The Flash]], and the shrinking problem of [[Atom (character)|the Atom]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.it.umn.edu/news/inventing/2002_Spring/superhero.html |title=Jim Kakalios:Superhero Science |work=Inventing Tomorrow |publisher=University of Minnesota Institute of Technology |year=2002 |accessdate=2006-07-10 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20060615181025/http://it.umn.edu/news/inventing/2002_Spring/superhero.html |archivedate=2006-06-15 }}</ref>  His analysis of Gwen Stacy's death eventually became integral to the plot of a new Spider-Man comic.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=4851397 |title=NPR: The Physics of Superheroes |accessdate= 2006-07-10|date=2006-09-25 |format=Windows Media |work=Talk of the Nation |publisher=National Public Radio}}</ref>
Kakalios is of the opinion that the most unrealistic aspect of the comic-book universe is often the sociology.  He notes that pedestrians do not usually provide running monologues describing everything around them.  There is one aspect of the story of the Atom that he does not question, however.  The Atom begins as a physics professor, who encounters a chunk of [[white dwarf star]] and picks it up.  "By a conservative estimate, he is lifting about 5000 metric tons.  This is not unreasonable. We physics professors are just that strong."{{citation needed|date=October 2014}}

He provides content on the DVD of the film ''[[Watchmen (2009 film)|Watchmen]]''. Under extras, he is filmed discussing the physics of superheroes. As one of the film's lead scientific consultants of the 2012 film ''[[The Amazing Spider-Man (2012 film)|The Amazing Spider-Man]]'', Kakalios designed the film's "decay rate algorithm", which was inspired by the real-life [[Gompertz–Makeham law of mortality]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-06-28 |title=Physicist Contributes Equation Central to Upcoming Spider-man Film |url=http://physicsbuzz.physicscentral.com/2012/06/physicist-contributes-equation-central.html |website=Physics Central |publisher=American Physics Society |access-date=2020-08-18}}</ref>

Kakalios has been nominated by the [[University of Minnesota]] to be one of the [[USA Science and Engineering Festival]]'s Nifty Fifty Speakers who will speak about his work and career to middle and high school students in October 2010.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.usasciencefestival.org/index.php?option%3Dcom_content%26view%3Darticle%26id%3D74%26Itemid%3D95 |title=Nifty Fifty |accessdate=2012-10-20 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120723105635/http://www.usasciencefestival.org/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=74&Itemid=95 |archivedate=2012-07-23 }} retrieved 2010-03-26</ref>

James Kakalios was awarded an Honorary Doctor of Science degree from the [[University of Lincoln]], UK (2017).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.lincoln.ac.uk/news/2017/08/1387.asp|title=Explore 'The Uncanny Physics of Superhero Comic Books' in free public lecture|last=Lincoln|first=University of|website=University of Lincoln Press Office|language=en|access-date=2017-09-09}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|last=University of Lincoln|title=University of Lincoln September Graduation – 7 September 2017, 2:30pm ceremony|date=2017-09-07|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NpOWqEBVrns |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211219/NpOWqEBVrns |archive-date=2021-12-19 |url-status=live|accessdate=2017-09-09}}{{cbignore}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=http://lincolnmathsphys.wordpress.com/2017/09/07/superhero-professor-james-kakalios-gets-an-honorary-degree/|title=Superhero professor, James Kakalios, gets an honorary degree|date=2017-09-07|work=Maths & Physics News|access-date=2017-09-11|language=en-US}}</ref>

He was also awarded the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science|AAAS]] Public Engagement with Science Award in 2014.
